Andrea Gammon Portland LD 698
Dear Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and esteemed members of the Housing and Economic Development Committee,
My name is Andrea Gammon, and I'm a voting resident of Portland, Maine.
I'm writing to support LD 698: An Act to Sustain Emergency Homeless Shelters in Maine.
Maine's emergency shelters provide critical care and services to vulnerable individuals and families. With the growing homelessness crisis in our state, shelters across Maine are struggling to match the need, leaving far too many people no choice but to sleep outside and in places not meant for human habitation. If even one shelter closes, it will strain an already overburdened system and worsen this crisis, leaving more people to compete for fewer resources, including shelter beds, housing navigators, and critical life-saving services.
MaineHousing reports that a shelter bed in Maine costs $102 a night to operate, yet the state's Shelter Operating Subsidy only provides Maine emergency shelters with $7 a bed per night. This figure has remained the same since 2016, meanwhile Maine's emergency shelters have faced rising costs from inflation and had to expand services to keep communities safe during the pandemic. LD 698 will critically increase this contribution to $18 a bed per night, helping to ensure Maine's emergency shelters remain open, accessible, and professionally operated.
Maine needs and deserves safe and accessible emergency shelters that can meet the needs of the growing number of individuals and families experiencing homelessness in our state. LD 698 will help to make this a reality.
Thank you.

State of Maine - 132nd Legislature Joint Standing Committee on Housing and Economic Development Testimony of Andrew Lardie on behalf of Tedford Housing (Brunswick, Maine)
March 18, 2025
Supporting LD698, "An Act to Sustain Emergency Homeless Shelters in Maine"
Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and members of the Committee on Housing and Economic Development:
My name is Andrew Lardie, and I am here on behalf of Tedford Housing. Tedford serves 40 towns and 150,000 residents in the southern midcoast through a range of programs to prevent homelessness and mitigate its impact. I appreciate the opportunity to testify in support of LD698, An Act to Sustain Emergency Homeless Shelters in Maine.
I'm also here with a group of shelter Directors who've been collaborating for months. Out of respect for the committee's time, many of them are submitting testimony in writing but not in person - so I want to acknowledge all of my colleagues now - can all our agency reps please stand for a moment?
Today you have heard from other presenters about the serious threat facing the shelter network, and thus to our shared quality of life in Maine. You have heard how first responders count on shelters doing our part, so that they can do their part and be ready to serve the whole community. You have heard the numbers verified by MaineHousing's Shelter Cost Study, of what it takes to provide shelter and get people back on their feet.
That study made it clear: this vital public health function is a lot more expensive to perform than the state has been paying. Whatever you think about the role of the state in supporting non-profits, the fact is: decent housing is a public good. And if this end of the housing spectrum is not sustained, the consequence is worse public health, more strain on the adjacent systems (eg hospitals, law enforcement, schools), a debilitated workforce, and a hobbled economy.
Emergency shelters are needed in communities across Maine to support people on their path back to housing. This bill won't make operating an emergency shelter profitable, or even break-even, but what it will do is to help Maine's shelters be more financially sustainable.
LD 698 is a critically important piece of legislation that will narrow the $95 gap that shelters need to fill from other sources for every bed, every night. At Tedford our shelter expansion, which the community badly needs, means the Operations pie will be divided into even smaller slices. But our total government funding sources already leave $59 per bednight to raise from philanthropy.
This funding will help keep Maine's shelters afloat as we all navigate the state's housing crisis. Today, on behalf of Maine's emergency shelters and the people we keep warm and safe every night, I am asking the Housing & Economic Development Committee to vote in favor of LD 698.
Andrew Lardie Executive Director Tedford Housing

Good afternoon, Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and members of the Committee on Housing and Economic Development,
My name is Terence Miller, and I am the Advocacy Director at Preble Street. Preble Street operates 16 programs throughout Maine, and its staff works daily alongside hundreds of individuals and families who struggle with housing insecurity. Our mission is to provide accessible, barrier-free services to empower people experiencing problems with homelessness, housing, hunger, and poverty and advocate for solutions to these problems.

TESTIMONY IN SUPPORT OF LD 698 AN ACT TO SUSTAIN EMERGENCY HOMELESS SHELTERS IN MAINE
Tuesday, March 18, 2025
Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and the esteemed members of the Committee on Housing and Economic Development. My name is Carter Friend and I am the CEO of York County Community Action. Our mission is to ensure that all people in York County thrive. We work with our partners to meet urgent needs, create opportunities to succeed, promote well-being, and advocate for just policies and practices. We strongly support LD 698, An Act to Sustain Emergency Homeless Shelters in Maine.
YCCAC is both a Community Action Agency and a Community Health Center. We have seen a dramatic increase in the number of clients and patients who are homeless or at high risk of homelessness. Nasson Health Care, our community health center, is a healthcare for the homeless provider. Last year, 1584 Nasson patients reported that they had experienced a period of homelessness within the past 12 months.
York County's emergency shelters are a vital resource for these and other members of our community. In York County we have one adult emergency shelter, one family emergency shelter and one domestic violence emergency shelter (these programs are run by two Emergency Shelter and Housing Assistance Program (ESHAP) providers). York County emergency shelters operate at full capacity, and they provide critical services such as substance use disorder treatment, case management and housing.
Yet emergency shelters do not receive the funding they need to sustain operations. The average cost to provide a bed night of shelter and associated services in Maine is $102 per person/per night across all ESHAP shelters. Currently, Maine's emergency shelters receive $7.16 per person/per night from the operations share of ESHAP funding, which leaves 93% of costs to be raised from other sources. This is unsustainable and has created a real risk that multiple shelters across the state will close. LD 698 would increase this funding to $19 per person/per night.
It is also important to highlight the critical role emergency shelters play in the Housing Continuum. Partners in York County work closely together every day to address homelessness. We have found that in order to be successful, we must address every part of the Housing Continuum - from prevention, to emergency shelter, to housing, and ultimately to homeownership. Emergency Shelters are a lynchpin of the continuum, helping people who are homeless meet their immediate need of safe shelter, and providing them with assistance and support to help them move along the continuum.
For these reasons, York County Community Action strongly urges you to support the passage of LD 698. Thank you for the hard work you do on behalf of Mainers.
Carter Friend, CEO York County Community Action Corporation

Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and members of the Housing and Economic Development Committee, my name is Cullen Ryan, and I am the Executive Director of Community Housing of Maine or CHOM. CHOM's small staff works collaboratively to create housing enriched with services to help people overcome challenges.
I am testifying in strong support of LD 698, An Act to Sustain Emergency Homeless Shelters in Maine. This bill provides ongoing funds to support emergency homeless shelters in the State - $5,000,000 in each year of the biennium.
Emergency shelters depend upon a variety of funding streams, that even when combined do not cover the cost of providing shelter. And, with additional shelter beds added to our system, the already insufficient funding has been stretched even thinner.
Shelters haven't had enough resources to maintain sufficient capacity and staffing to meet the need for years. Our shelters are in crisis. For Maine to safely meet the needs of people experiencing homelessness, we must have a robust, adequately funded shelter system - it is the foundation of our homeless service system.
Shelters in Maine have been full, operating overflow shelters, and/or forced to turn people away due to insurmountable capacity issues for years. And they are currently operating at large annual deficits - some as high as $855,000. Without additional funding allocations emergency shelters in Maine will close - some imminently (please see the attached document for additional information).
We need all of Maine's shelters to remain open, or we will most certainly see an exponential growth in encampments.
Maine is already on the precipice of widespread unsheltered homelessness. We experienced this briefly in 2023. Our shelter system is currently full, and it is starting to overflow. If shelters close or lose capacity, it will leave people with no choice but to congregate outside.
Encampments are not good for any city or town. Access to shelter and housing is.
It is extremely challenging to house people when they are outside because they are overwhelmed trying to survive each day and night. Having a shelter system with sufficient capacity allows the focus to shift from keeping people alive while outdoors (managing a life-threatening crisis) to housing people and keeping them housed (ending homelessness).
Emergency shelters provide a foundation from which people can be safe and focus on the complicated work of getting housed. Shelter staff are successful in assisting people with paperwork, and all the forms and appointments necessary to qualify for affordable housing.
Getting people housed creates cost savings for local, county, and state governments. People who are chronically homeless are up to 29 times more likely to be in the hospital and up to 57 times more likely to be in jail than when unhoused than when housed. It is 27 times more expensive to be in the hospital and 4 times more expensive to be in jail than in housing.

Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Housing and Economic Development, I am Deborah Laurie, City Manager of the City of Bangor. On behalf of the Bangor City Council I am providing testimony in support of LD 698, "An Act to Sustain Emergency Homeless Shelters in Maine."

The roughly 93% gap in funds must be made up via other means like General Assistance, fundraising, endowments, etc.
This shortfall in funds further stresses operations capacity as shelters must still account for workforce challenges, rising costs in food and utilities, and the associated challenges of continued stagnation within the homeless services continuum. Additional financial supports are needed now, particularly as the inflow of folks experiencing homelessness into the system is outpacing our ability to access available permanent housing options for people to exit the continuum.
The funding allocated in LD 698 will not alleviate the struggle Maine's emergency shelters continue to face, but it is a necessary first step. Increasing the Operations Subsidy to $19 per bednight, as proposed via the $5M in funding from LD 698, will aid shelters in starting to reverse deficits and increase breathing room in budgets and will better enable emergency shelters to serve those in need across Maine.

Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and members of the Committee on Housing and Economic Development:
My name is Lily Lynch, I am testifying on behalf of The Opportunity Alliance and my community in support of this legislation. I appreciate the opportunity to testify in support of LD698, An Act to Sustain Emergency Homeless Shelters in Maine.
At The Opportunity Alliance, our 450 employees across dozens of programs work with more than 24,000 low-income Mainers each year to keep them safe and healthy and help them thrive. Each year TOA programs such as Mobile Crisis Unit, Broadway Crossings Adult Crisis Stabilization Unit, Project for Assistance in Transition from Homelessness (PATH), Homeless Youth Services, and Cumberland County Homeless Prevention Program provide targeted interventions for individuals and families experiencing housing instability. Given the current housing crisis, we're also seeing housing instability impact clients within many of our other programs, such as Head Start, WIC, and case management.
The role of housing as a social determinant of health is well established, and the severe lack of housing in Maine has exacerbated the mental health crisis. Unstable housing situations or lack of shelter make it impossible for individuals to maintain jobs, stay engaged in school, and be connected members of their community. Research shows that homelessness is costly for communities and systems of care, as individuals who are unsheltered are more likely to utilize emergency rooms and public safety and crisis response services.
Shelters provide an important opportunity for individuals and families to stabilize a crisis and seek additional support. Shelters also provide a critical touchpoint where case managers and service providers can reach individuals and families and build important relationships. When individuals or families are unhoused and transient, gains made in finding housing, mental health and substance use support, education, and access to basic needs can be set back days, weeks, or even months.
Collaboration is a cornerstone of TOA's success; programs work in partnership with the client(s), community organizations, and service providers, including many shelters across the state. If shelters were to close, we believe it would be detrimental to the people we serve and residents across Maine.
Please vote Ought to Pass on LD698, so Maine's social service agencies can focus on our mission and build a community in which all people in Maine have access to high-quality

childcare and early childhood education programs, safe and stable housing, effective and compassionate mental health and substance use treatment, and basic needs supports. Thank you for your consideration.

Senator Curry, Representative Gere, and the esteemed members of the Committee on Housing and Economic Development. My name is Megan Gean-Gendron, Executive Director of York County Shelter Programs - York County's only emergency adult and family shelter. I am submitting this testimony in support of LD 698 An Act to Sustain Emergency Homeless Shelters in Maine. I am deeply concerned about the state of our emergency homeless shelters, as they play a critical role in providing basic needs, stability, and hope to some of Maine's most vulnerable citizens. However, the funding allocated to these shelters is far from sufficient to meet the actual costs of providing safe and supportive housing at a time when the State of Maine is faced with a homelessness and housing crisis putting even more of a demand on this critical services.
Currently, homeless shelters in Maine are funded at a rate of only $7.16 per night per individual. This amount is far below the actual cost of providing shelter and services, which averages around $102 per night per person. This funding gap creates immense challenges for shelters to deliver the quality of care, support, and services that our community members in crisis so desperately need and leaves emergency homeless shelters to raise 93% of their budgets from other sources. This is unsustainable and has put the shelter system at great risk with multiple shelters around the state with soaring deficits and a threat of closure.
The disparity between the allocated funding and the actual cost of running a shelter impacts the services that are essential for people experiencing homelessness. Without adequate funding, shelters are forced to reduce staff at a time when we need to increase the number of beds in shelters, limit access to services such as case management, mental health support, and addiction recovery programs, or even turn people away when they are most vulnerable. This, in turn, leads to higher rates of individuals and families becoming unsheltered or facing long-term instability.
Homelessness is not just a housing issue; it is a complex, multi-faceted problem that requires coordinated responses across housing, healthcare, mental health, addiction services, and employment support. Without sufficient funding for shelters, the broader network of services becomes less effective, and individuals remain trapped in a cycle of crisis. For some, this could mean their homelessness becomes chronic, with lifelong impacts on their physical and mental well-being.
The $7.16 per night per person is not nearly enough to address the full scope of the challenges that shelters are facing. Maine's shelters need adequate funding to ensure they can provide not only a bed for the night but also the comprehensive care and services that will help individuals get back on their feet and rebuild their lives. LD 698 could increase that operational gap from $7.16 per night to $19 per night of the $102 cost of that bed.

My name is Shannon Shimer and I am the Assistant Director of Social Services at Homeworthy. I am writing to express my fervent support for proposed L.D. 698 regarding Emergency Shelters Funding. In my role at Homeworthy, I support and supervise seven of the 14 case managers in our office. In this current housing climate, I often spend many hours per week strategizing with case managers for the ways to support clients' connection to emergency shelter beds statewide.
I cannot underscore enough how vital shelters are for our neighbors who are experiencing homelessness. Many situations may occur that result in a person needing emergency shelter, including receiving an eviction notice, fleeing domestic violence, the loss of a job and inability to pay rent, someone struggling with substance misuse, and medical incidents that zap someone of their savings. At Homeworthy, we are grateful to have the Hospitality House family shelter, which is an incredible resource in the area but unfortunately does not meet the overwhelming shelter needs of our community.
Many of our clients have deep, multigenerational ties to the area and wish to remain in the midcoast to be closer to employment, family, friends, medical providers, and other social supports. When Hospitality House does not have availability to shelter clients of ours, my first phone call is always to H.O.M.E. Inc. in Orland, which is one hour north of Homeworthy. If H.O.M.E. Inc. is not available, my second phone call is to Tedford Housing in Brunswick--one hour south in the opposite direction of Homeworthy. Consistently, both shelters are full and carrying their own waitlist of clients seeking shelter.
I would like to share a real life example of a client who is currently experiencing homelessness and how their situation is being impacted by the difficulty accessing a shelter bed. We have a client who is a single parent with two school aged children. They have been living in a local motel paid for by General Assistance since early autumn last year. General Assistance cut off their funding in early January after they far exceeded the limits of what their town was legally able to offer. The parent really struggles to complete basic daily tasks and has a Daily Living Skills (DLS) worker who comes once a week to assist them. They rely heavily on their case manager, child's case manager, and the DLS worker to assign and support the client to follow through on tasks including sourcing groceries, following through on referrals and medical appointments, provide Child Protective Services advocacy, and other essential tasks. One of their children has significant behavioral problems and receives a lot of steady, consistent support from their school's special education department. Our shelter has

not had a room available for this family since they entered the waiting list in September 2024. In the meantime, this client has been piecing together motel funding on a weekly and sometimes nightly basis in order to stay close to family supports and for the children to remain in their current school. This client has to move out of their motel room this week due to funding and has nowhere to go. They are currently facing splitting up the children and the client is considering moving into a tent in order to remain in the area.
We are at a real crossroads in Maine about how our state supports and sustains homeless shelters. LD 698 acknowledges what we all know to be true: that emergency shelters are expensive to operate, that the need far outpaces the supply, and that even as we invest in long-term housing solutions, people will continue to fall through the cracks. We must ensure that, when they do, there is a safe place to land. I support this bill, but I do so with the full awareness that it is not the solution. It is a response. A response to crisis, to human suffering, to the reality that we, as a society, have yet to do enough upstream to prevent the need for these warehouses in the first place. As someone who has lived through the experience of homelessness, I understand how shelters can serve as a temporary reprieve, but they are often not the path to a full and lasting solution. Our goal must always be to create housing stability, supportive services, and the opportunity for individuals to regain their autonomy and dignity. So yes, let us pass LD 698. But let us also commit to the work beyond it. The work of making these emergency measures less necessary. The work of housing, of stability, of recovery - of dignity. The work of ensuring that, one day, we will not need warehouses at all. Thank you.
Jason Goodrich Brewer Maine
